claim: The anterior rhombencephalic turning region (ARTR) is a circuit that controls zebrafish swimming statistics.
source: Here, we infer an energy-based model of the anterior rhombencephalic turning region (ARTR), a circuit that controls zebrafish swimming statistics, using functional recordings of the spontaneous activity of hundreds of neurons.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of the ARTR circuit.

claim: The energy-based model is trained to reproduce the low-order statistics of the network activity at short time scales.
source: Although our model is trained to reproduce the low-order statistics of the network activity at short time scales, its simulated dynamics quantitatively captures the slowly alternating activity of the ARTR.
evidence: This describes the training methodology of the model.

claim: The model's simulated dynamics quantitatively captures the slowly alternating activity of the ARTR.
source: Although our model is trained to reproduce the low-order statistics of the network activity at short time scales, its simulated dynamics quantitatively captures the slowly alternating activity of the ARTR.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrating the model's predictive capacity.

claim: The model reproduces the modulation of persistent dynamics by water temperature.
source: It further reproduces the modulation of this persistent dynamics by the water temperature and visual stimulation.
evidence: This is a key result showing the model captures temperature-dependent behavior.

claim: The model reproduces the modulation of persistent dynamics by visual stimulation.
source: It further reproduces the modulation of this persistent dynamics by the water temperature and visual stimulation.
evidence: This demonstrates the model's capacity to capture stimulus-driven dynamics.

claim: Mathematical analysis of the model unveils a low-dimensional landscape-based representation of the ARTR activity.
source: Mathematical analysis of the model unveils a low-dimensional landscape-based representation of the ARTR activity, where the slow network dynamics reflects Arrhenius-like barriers crossings between metastable states.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach and its outcome.

claim: The slow network dynamics reflects Arrhenius-like barriers crossings between metastable states.
source: Mathematical analysis of the model unveils a low-dimensional landscape-based representation of the ARTR activity, where the slow network dynamics reflects Arrhenius-like barriers crossings between metastable states.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation derived from the mean-field analysis.

claim: Machine-learning models trained on recorded activity allow for the decoding or prediction of neuronal activity and behavior.
source: Machine-learning models, trained on recorded activity, allow for the decoding or the prediction of neuronal activity and behavior (Glaser et al., 2020; Pandarinath et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The blackbox nature of data-driven models often obscures their biological interpretation.
source: Unfortunately, the blackbox nature of these data-driven models often obscures their biological interpretation, for example, the identification of the relevant computational units (Butts, 2019).
evidence: This is a known limitation cited from the literature.

claim: The ARTR drives the saccadic dynamics and orchestrates the chaining of leftward/rightward swim bouts.
source: This work is an attempt to do so in the specific context of the anterior rhombencephalic turning region (ARTR), a circuit in the zebrafish larva that drives the saccadic dynamics and orchestrates the chaining of leftward/rightward swim bouts (Ahrens et al., 2013; Dunn et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2017; Ramirez and Aksay, 2021; Leyden et al., 2021).
evidence: This functional characterization is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The ARTR spontaneous activity exhibits temporal persistence over long (~10 s) time scales.
source: The ARTR spontaneous activity exhibits temporal persistence, that is, the maintenance of activity patterns over long (∼ 10 s) time scales.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data.

claim: Temporal persistence is ubiquitous in the vertebrate brain.
source: This functional feature is ubiquitous in the vertebrate brain.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Temporal persistence plays an essential role in motor control.
source: It plays an essential role in motor control, as best exemplified by the velocity position neural integrator, a circuit that integrates neural inputs and allows for a maintenance of the eye position after an ocular saccade (Seung, 1996; Seung et al., 2000; Miri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to work on neural integrators.

claim: Temporal persistence is central to action selection.
source: Temporal persistence is also central to action selection (Wang, 2008) and short-term memory storage (Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Temporal persistence is central to short-term memory storage.
source: Temporal persistence is also central to action selection (Wang, 2008) and short-term memory storage (Zaksas and Pasternak, 2006; Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Neural persistence is thought to be an emergent property of recurrent circuit architectures.
source: As isolated neurons generally display short relaxation times, neural persistence is thought to be an emergent property of recurrent circuit architectures (Zylberberg and Strowbridge, 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical perspective supported by citation.

claim: Energy-based network models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in the retina.
source: In neuroscience, such models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in many areas, including the retina (Schneidman et al., 2006; Cocco et al., 2009; Tkačik et al., 2015), the cortex (Tavoni et al., 2016; Tavoni et al., 2017; Nghiem et al., 2018), and the hippocampus (Meshulam et al., 2017; Posani et al., 2017) of vertebrates, and the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Energy-based network models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in the cortex.
source: In neuroscience, such models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in many areas, including the retina (Schneidman et al., 2006; Cocco et al., 2009; Tkačik et al., 2015), the cortex (Tavoni et al., 2016; Tavoni et al., 2017; Nghiem et al., 2018), and the hippocampus (Meshulam et al., 2017; Posani et al., 2017) of vertebrates, and the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Energy-based network models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in the hippocampus.
source: In neuroscience, such models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in many areas, including the retina (Schneidman et al., 2006; Cocco et al., 2009; Tkačik et al., 2015), the cortex (Tavoni et al., 2016; Tavoni et al., 2017; Nghiem et al., 2018), and the hippocampus (Meshulam et al., 2017; Posani et al., 2017) of vertebrates, and the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Energy-based network models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: In neuroscience, such models have been successfully used to explain correlation structures in many areas, including the retina (Schneidman et al., 2006; Cocco et al., 2009; Tkačik et al., 2015), the cortex (Tavoni et al., 2016; Tavoni et al., 2017; Nghiem et al., 2018), and the hippocampus (Meshulam et al., 2017; Posani et al., 2017) of vertebrates, and the nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The water temperature controls the persistence time scale of the ARTR network.
source: These data demonstrate that the water temperature controls the persistence time scale of the ARTR network, and that this modulation is in quantitative agreement with the thermal dependence of the swimming statistics.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding.

claim: The thermal modulation of ARTR persistence is in quantitative agreement with the thermal dependence of swimming statistics.
source: These data demonstrate that the water temperature controls the persistence time scale of the ARTR network, and that this modulation is in quantitative agreement with the thermal dependence of the swimming statistics.
evidence: This establishes a quantitative relationship between neural and behavioral data.

claim: The inferred energy-based models capture the characteristics and probabilities of occurrence of activity patterns.
source: We then infer energy-based models from the calcium activity recordings and show how these data-driven models not only capture the characteristics and probabilities of occurrence of activity patterns, but also reproduce the observed thermal dependence of the persistent time scale.
evidence: This is a key result demonstrating the model's accuracy.

claim: The inferred energy-based models reproduce the observed thermal dependence of the persistent time scale.
source: We then infer energy-based models from the calcium activity recordings and show how these data-driven models not only capture the characteristics and probabilities of occurrence of activity patterns, but also reproduce the observed thermal dependence of the persistent time scale.
evidence: This is a key result showing the model captures temperature effects.

claim: Light-sheet functional imaging was used to record ARTR activity in zebrafish larvae at various temperatures (18–33°C).
source: We used light-sheet functional imaging to record the ARTR activity in zebrafish larvae expressing a calcium reporter pan-neuronally (Tg(elavl3:GCaMP6)). The larvae, embedded in agarose, were placed in a water tank whose temperature was controlled in the range 18–33°C (see Appendix 2—figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: ARTR neurons were identified using a combination of morphological and functional criteria.
source: ARTR neurons were identified using a combination of morphological and functional criteria, as detailed in Wolf et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes the neuron selection methodology with citation.

claim: The recordings included 145 ± 65 left neurons and 165 ± 69 right neurons (mean ± SD across 13 different fish).
source: Their spatial organization is displayed in Figure 1A, for all recorded animals after morphological registration on a unique reference brain (145 ± 65 left neurons, 165 ± 69 right neurons, mean ± SD across 13 different fish, see Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: This provides quantitative data about the recorded neurons.

claim: The alternation frequency ν was found to increase with temperature.
source: This frequency was found to increase with the temperature (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in the data and figure.

claim: The flipping rate kflip systematically increases with temperature, from 0.1 to 0.6 s−1.
source: This rate, which defines the probability of switching orientation per unit of time, systematically increases with the temperature, from 0.1 to 0.6 s−1 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from behavioral data.

claim: Increasing the temperature leads to a progressive reduction of the turn direction persistence time.
source: Increasing the temperature thus leads to a progressive reduction of the turn direction persistence time.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in flipping rate with temperature.

claim: At lower temperature, the ARTR activity is characterized by long periods during which both circuits are active and shorter periods of inactivity.
source: Conversely, at lower temperature, the ARTR activity is characterized by long periods during which both circuits are active and shorter periods of inactivity.
evidence: This is an observation from the probability maps in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no clear dependency of the average correlation across ipsilateral or contralateral pairs of neurons with temperature.
source: In order to test this, we computed the Pearson correlation at various temperature but we saw no clear dependency of the average correlation across ipsilateral or contralateral pairs of neurons (Appendix 2—figure 2C).
evidence: This is a negative result from the correlation analysis.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between the persistence time and the mean activity across animals and trials for a given temperature.
source: Nevertheless, we observed a strong positive correlation between the persistence time and the mean activity across animals and trials for a given temperature (Appendix 2—figure 2D and 'Materials and methods'), indicating that both features of the ARTR may have a common drive.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding suggesting a mechanistic relationship.

claim: The synthetic signals generated by the Ising model exhibit the main characteristics of the ARTR dynamics, including slow alternation between left and right subpopulations with long persistence times.
source: Remarkably, although the Ising model is trained to reproduce the low-order statistics of the neuronal activity within a time bin only, the generated signals exhibit the main characteristics of the ARTR dynamics, that is, a slow alternation between the left and right subpopulations associated with long persistence times; see raster plots in Figure 2C.
evidence: This is a key finding showing emergent dynamics in the model.

claim: The Ising model quantitatively reproduces the ARTR activity distribution associated to each specimen and temperature.
source: This result establishes that the Ising model quantitatively reproduces the ARTR activity distribution associated to each specimen and temperature.
evidence: This is based on the KL divergence analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The agreement between model and data crucially relies on the presence of inter-neuronal couplings.
source: This agreement crucially relies on the presence of inter-neuronal couplings in order to reproduce the pairwise correlations in the activity: a model with no connection (i.e., the independent model, see 'Materials and methods') fitted to reproduce the neural firing rates offers a very poor description of the data (see Figure 3A [dark blue distribution] and Appendix 2—figure 3E–G).
evidence: This demonstrates the importance of couplings through comparison with independent model.

claim: The MC dynamics captures the inter-individual variability and temperature dependence of the ARTR persistent dynamics.
source: The MC dynamics thus captures the inter-individual variability and temperature dependence of the ARTR persistent dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the strong correlation between data and model persistence times.

claim: Inferred ipsilateral couplings are centered around a positive value (std = 0.12, mean = 0.062).
source: In all recordings, inferred ipsilateral couplings are found to be centered around a positive value (std = 0.12, mean = 0.062), while contralateral couplings are distributed around 0 (mean = –0.001, std = 0.10); see Appendix 2—figure 4A–C.
evidence: This provides quantitative characterization of the inferred couplings.

claim: Contralateral couplings are distributed around 0 (mean = –0.001, std = 0.10).
source: In all recordings, inferred ipsilateral couplings are found to be centered around a positive value (std = 0.12, mean = 0.062), while contralateral couplings are distributed around 0 (mean = –0.001, std = 0.10); see Appendix 2—figure 4A–C.
evidence: This provides quantitative characterization of the inferred couplings.

claim: A significant fraction of contralateral couplings are strongly negative.
source: Still, a significant fraction of these contralateral couplings are strongly negative.
evidence: This is an observation from the coupling distribution analysis.

claim: Large negative values of couplings or correlations systematically correspond to contralateral pairs of neurons.
source: Large negative values of couplings or correlations systematically correspond to contralateral pairs of neurons, whereas large positive values correspond to ipsilateral pairs of neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the analysis of coupling and correlation distributions.

claim: Large positive values of couplings or correlations correspond to ipsilateral pairs of neurons.
source: Large negative values of couplings or correlations systematically correspond to contralateral pairs of neurons, whereas large positive values correspond to ipsilateral pairs of neurons.
evidence: This is shown in the analysis of coupling and correlation distributions.

claim: Spatial structure is present in contralateral couplings.
source: Spatial structure is also present in contralateral couplings (Appendix 2—figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in the spatial analysis of couplings.

claim: Biases display a wide distribution ranging from –8 to 0 (std = 1.1, mean = –4.1).
source: Biases display a wide distribution ranging from –8 to 0 (std = 1.1, mean = –4.1, Appendix 2—figure 5A–C), with no apparent spatial structure.
evidence: This provides quantitative characterization of the inferred biases.

claim: Biases have no apparent spatial structure.
source: Biases display a wide distribution ranging from –8 to 0 (std = 1.1, mean = –4.1, Appendix 2—figure 5A–C), with no apparent spatial structure.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial analysis of biases.

claim: The minima of the free energy define persistent states of activity in which the network can be transiently trapped.
source: In particular, the minima of the free energy define persistent states of activity in which the network can be transiently trapped.
evidence: This is a consequence of the free energy landscape interpretation.

claim: At high temperature, only the low–low activity state is accessible in practice to the system.
source: As a consequence, at high temperature, only the low–low activity state is accessible in practice to the system, and the mean activity remains low (see Appendix 2—figure 2D), with fluctuations within the low–low state.
evidence: This is inferred from the barrier height analysis.

claim: At low water temperatures, barriers separating the low–low and the active high–low or low–high states are weaker, so the latter become accessible.
source: Conversely, at low water temperatures, barriers separating the low–low and the active high–low or low–high states are weaker, so the latter become accessible.
evidence: This is inferred from the barrier height analysis.

claim: The mean activity is higher at low temperature.
source: As a first consequence, the mean activity is higher at low temperature (Appendix 2—figure 2D).
evidence: This is a consequence of the accessible states at low temperature.

claim: The system remains trapped for some time in an active state before switching to the other side at low temperature, which is the origin of the longer persistence time.
source: Furthermore, the system remains trapped for some time in such an active state before switching to the other side, for example, from high–low to low–high. This is the origin of the longer persistence time observed at low temperature.
evidence: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the temperature-dependent persistence.

claim: The ARTR activity could be driven by alternating unilateral visual stimulation: the right side of the ARTR tended to activate when the right eye was stimulated and vice versa.
source: We found that the ARTR activity could be driven by this alternating unilateral visual stimulation: the right side of the ARTR tended to activate when the right eye was stimulated and vice versa (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the visual stimulation experiments.

claim: Light stimulation produces a strong increase of excitability for the ipsilateral neurons and a smaller one for contralateral neurons.
source: The results show that light stimulation produces a strong increase of excitability for the ipsilateral neurons and a smaller one for contralateral neurons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D from the inferred additional biases.

claim: The simulated dynamics of the model qualitatively reproduces the experimental traces of the ARTR activity under visual stimulation.
source: The simulated dynamics of the model (Figure 5E) qualitatively reproduces the experimental traces of the ARTR activity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This demonstrates the model's capacity to capture visually driven dynamics.

claim: Due to the extra bias from visual stimulation, the left- or right-active states are much more likely, and the barrier separating them from the low–low state is much lower.
source: Due to the presence of the extra bias, the landscape is tilted with respect to its no-stimulation counterpart (Figure 5G), entailing that the left- or right-active states are much more likely, and the barrier separating them from the low–low state is much lower.
evidence: This is shown in the mean-field analysis of the stimulated condition.

claim: The time necessary for reaching the high-activity state is considerably reduced with respect to the no-stimulation case under visual stimulation.
source: As a consequence, the time necessary for reaching the high-activity state is considerably reduced with respect to the no-stimulation case (see Equation 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced barrier height under stimulation.

claim: The persistent time scale of the ARTR endogenous dynamics decreases with the temperature, mirroring the thermal modulation of turn direction persistence in freely swimming behavioral assays.
source: First, we demonstrate that the persistent time scale of the ARTR endogenous dynamics decreases with the temperature, mirroring the thermal modulation of turn direction persistence in freely swimming behavioral assays.
evidence: This is a primary finding summarizing the neural-behavioral relationship.

claim: The brains of cold-blooded animals need to operate within the range of temperature that they experience in their natural habitat (18–33°C for zebrafish).
source: The brains of cold-blooded animals need to operate within the range of temperature that they experience in their natural habitat, for example, 18–33°C for zebrafish (Gau et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a general statement about cold-blooded animals with citation for zebrafish.

claim: An increase in temperature tends to increase the frequency of oscillatory processes in general.
source: Yet in general, an increase in temperature tends to increase the frequency of oscillatory processes (Robertson and Money, 2012).
evidence: This is a general principle supported by citation.

claim: The observed acceleration of the ARTR left/right alternation with increasing temperature could directly result from temperature-dependent cellular mechanisms.
source: The observed acceleration of the ARTR left/right alternation with increasing temperature could thus directly result from temperature-dependent cellular mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the temperature effect.

claim: The ARTR dynamics could be indirectly modulated by temperature via thermal-dependent descending neuromodulatory inputs.
source: Furthermore, one cannot rule out the possibility that the ARTR dynamics could also be indirectly modulated by temperature via thermal-dependent descending neuromodulatory inputs.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative mechanism.

claim: Many cold-blooded animals exhibit temperature dependence of their behavior.
source: As a result of this thermal modulation of the neuronal dynamics, many cold-blooded animals also exhibit temperature dependence of their behavior (Long and Fee, 2008; Neumeister et al., 2000; Stevenson and Josephson, 1990).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations.

claim: The thermal dependence of the swimming kinematic endows the larva with basic thermophobic capacity, efficiently protecting them from exposure to the hottest regions of their environment.
source: Nevertheless, we were able to show in a recent study that this thermal dependence of the swimming kinematic endows the larva with basic thermophobic capacity, thus efficiently protecting them from exposure to the hottest regions of their environment (Le Goc et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The graphical model was trained to capture the low-order statistics of snapshots of activity and is blind to the dynamical nature of the population activity.
source: The graphical model we introduced in this work was trained to capture the low-order statistics of snapshots of activity. Because graphical models are blind to the dynamical nature of the population activity, it is generally believed that they cannot reproduce any dynamical feature.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the modeling approach.

claim: The model can quantitatively replicate aspects of the network long-term dynamics such as the slow alternation between the two preferred states.
source: Nevertheless, here we demonstrate that our model can quantitatively replicate aspects of the network long-term dynamics such as the slow alternation between the two preferred states.
evidence: This is a key finding that challenges conventional expectations.

claim: The MC algorithm cannot reproduce the correlations between successive time bins in the recording data at short time scales.
source: At short time scale, defined here as the duration of a time bin (of the order of a few 100 ms), the model cannot capture any meaningful dynamics. The MC algorithm we used to generate activity is an abstract and arbitrary process, and the correlations it produces between successive time bins cannot reproduce the ones in the recording data.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the model at short time scales.

claim: Capturing the short-term dynamics would require a biologically grounded model of the cell–cell interactions or parameters capturing the experimental temporal correlations over short time scales.
source: Capturing the short-term dynamics would require a biologically grounded model of the cell–cell interactions, or, at the very least, to introduce parameters capturing the experimental temporal correlations over this short time scale (Marre et al., 2009; Mézard and Sakellariou, 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations.

claim: The inability of the Ising model to reproduce short time dynamical correlations does not hinder its capacity to predict long-time behavior.
source: Yet, the inability of the Ising model to reproduce short time dynamical correlations does not hinder its capacity to predict long-time behavior.
evidence: This is a key insight about the model's capabilities.

claim: The separation between individual neuronal processes (taking place over time scales smaller than 100 ms) and network-scale activity modulation (happening on time scales ranging from 1 to 20 s) is essential.
source: The separation between individual neuronal processes (taking place over time scales smaller than 100 ms) and network-scale activity modulation, which happens on time scales ranging from 1 to 20 s, is here essential.
evidence: This explains why the model can capture long-term dynamics despite short-term limitations.

claim: In the mean-field version of the inferred Ising model, the slow dynamics reflects the itinerant exploration of a two-dimensional energy landscape.
source: Here, the slow dynamics reflects the itinerant exploration of a two-dimensional energy landscape (Figure 4C), for which the barriers separating metastable states scale linearly with the system size.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation from the mean-field analysis.

claim: The barriers separating metastable states scale linearly with the system size.
source: Here, the slow dynamics reflects the itinerant exploration of a two-dimensional energy landscape (Figure 4C), for which the barriers separating metastable states scale linearly with the system size.
evidence: This is a theoretical result from the mean-field analysis.

claim: The time to cross barriers grows exponentially with the system size, as prescribed by Arrhenius law, and can be orders of magnitude larger than any single-neuron relaxation time.
source: The time to cross these barriers in turn grows exponentially with the system size, as prescribed by Arrhenius law, and can be orders of magnitude larger than any single-neuron relaxation time.
evidence: This is a theoretical consequence of the barrier scaling.

claim: Persistence is an emerging property of the neural network.
source: Persistence is therefore an emerging property of the neural network.
evidence: This is a key conclusion about the mechanism of persistence.

claim: The mean-field approach allows unveiling the fundamental network features controlling the coarse-grained dynamics through a drastic simplification of the Ising model.
source: The mean-field approach, through a drastic simplification of the Ising model, allows us to unveil the fundamental network features controlling its coarse-grained dynamics.
evidence: This describes the utility of the mean-field approximation.

claim: Within the mean-field approximation, the distributions of couplings and of biases are replaced by their average values.
source: Within this approximation, the distributions of couplings and of biases are replaced by their average values.
evidence: This describes the mean-field approximation procedure.

claim: The heterogeneities characterizing the Ising model parameters, ignored in the mean-field approach, may play an important role in the network dynamics.
source: The heterogeneities characterizing the Ising model parameters (Appendix 2—figure 4 and Appendix 2—figure 5), and ignored in the mean-field approach, may, however, play an important role in the network dynamics.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the mean-field approximation.

claim: The ipsilateral couplings in the Ising model are broadly distributed such as to possess both negative and positive values.
source: In the Ising model, the ipsilateral couplings are found to be broadly distributed such as to possess both negative and positive values.
evidence: This is an observation from the inferred parameters.

claim: The broad distribution of ipsilateral couplings leads to the presence of frustrated loops in the network.
source: This leads to the presence of so-called frustrated loops, that is, chains of neurons along which the product of the pairwise couplings is negative.
evidence: This is a consequence of the coupling distribution.

claim: The states of activities of neurons along frustrated loops cannot be set in a way that satisfies all the excitatory and inhibitory connections, giving rise to dynamical instabilities.
source: The states of activities of the neurons along such loops cannot be set in a way that satisfies all the excitatory and inhibitory connections, hence giving rise to dynamical instabilities in the states of the neurons.
evidence: This explains the consequence of frustrated loops.

claim: Contralateral couplings show strong correlations for short distances between the contralateral neurons.
source: Similarly, contralateral couplings show strong correlations for short distances between the contralateral neurons (Appendix 2—figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of couplings.

claim: The existence of a local spatial organization in the couplings can have important functional consequences and is at the basis of ring-like attractor models.
source: The existence of a local spatial organization in the couplings is not unheard of in computational neuroscience and can have important functional consequences. It is, for instance, at the basis of ring-like attractor models and their extensions to two or three dimensions (Tsodyks and Sejnowski, 1995).
evidence: This relates the findings to known computational neuroscience concepts with citation.

claim: An avalanche mechanism could explain the fast rise of activity in the left or right region, from low- to high-activity state.
source: As the most excitable neurons (with the largest biases) fire, they excite their neighbors, who in turn become active, triggering the activation of other neurons in their neighborhood. Such an avalanche mechanism could explain the fast rise of activity in the left or right region, from low- to high-activity state.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation.

claim: The spatial distribution of functional couplings appears to be in line with the known ARTR organization characterized by large positive interactions within left and right populations and negative contralateral interactions.
source: However, their spatial distribution appears to be in line with the known ARTR organization (Dunn et al., 2016; Kinkhabwala et al., 2011) characterized by large positive (excitatory) interactions within the left and right population, and by the presence of negative (inhibitory) contralateral interactions.
evidence: This relates the inferred parameters to known anatomy with citations.

claim: The contralateral couplings drive a subtle interplay between the left and right regions of the ARTR.
source: Although the contralateral couplings are found to be, on average, almost null, compared to the ipsilateral excitatory counterparts, they drive a subtle interplay between the left and right regions of the ARTR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the role of contralateral couplings.

claim: The model correctly captures the thermal modulation of the ARTR activity, including the decay of the persistence time with temperature.
source: The model correctly captures this thermal modulation of the ARTR activity, and in particular the decay of the persistence time with the temperature.
evidence: This is a key result demonstrating the model's accuracy.

claim: The thermal modulation owes to a progressive change in the values of both the couplings and the biases, which together deform the energy landscape and modulate the energy barriers between metastable states.
source: This owes to a progressive change in the values of both the couplings and the biases, which together deform the energy landscape and modulate the energy barriers between metastable states.
evidence: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the temperature effect.

claim: The fact that the inferred functional connectivity between neurons does not display simple temperature dependence is not unexpected as different membrane currents can have different temperature dependence.
source: The fact that the inferred functional connectivity between neurons does not display simple temperature dependence is not unexpected as different membrane currents can have different temperature dependence (Partridge and Connor, 1978).
evidence: This explains the complex temperature dependence with citation.

claim: The inferred parameters largely vary across datasets.
source: In addition, as shown in Appendix 2—table 2, the inferred parameters largely vary across datasets.
evidence: This is an observation from the inference results.

claim: Recent studies have shown that spontaneous behavior in zebrafish larvae exhibits transitions between different regimes lasting over minutes and associated with specific brain states.
source: Recent studies have shown that spontaneous behavior in zebrafish larvae is not time-invariant but exhibits transitions between different regimes, lasting over minutes and associated with specific brain states.
evidence: This is a general statement about zebrafish behavior.

claim: Behavioral transitions can have no apparent cause or be induced by external or internal cues.
source: These transitions can have no apparent cause (Le Goc et al., 2021) or be induced by external (e.g., stimuli; Andalman et al., 2019) or internal cues (e.g., hunger states; Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Behavioral transitions engage brain-wide changes in the pattern of spontaneous neural dynamics and are often triggered by the activation of neuromodulatory centers such as the habenula-dorsal raphe nucleus circuit.
source: Although they engage brain-wide changes in the pattern of spontaneous neural dynamics, they are often triggered by the activation of neuromodulatory centers such as the habenula-dorsal raphe nucleus circuit (Corradi and Filosa, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Training Ising models in various conditions may help decipher how neuromodulation impacts the network functional couplings leading to distinct dynamical regimes of spontaneous activity.
source: Training Ising models in various conditions may help decipher how such neuromodulation impacts the network functional couplings leading to distinct dynamical regimes of spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a prospective statement about future applications.

claim: The ARTR offers an ideally suited circuit to test the capacity of Ising models to capture network-driven dynamics due to its slow alternating activity and relatively simple architecture.
source: With its slow alternating activity and relatively simple architecture, the ARTR offers an ideally suited circuit to test the capacity of Ising models to capture network-driven dynamics.
evidence: This explains why the ARTR was chosen for this study.

claim: The possibility to experimentally modulate the ARTR persistence time scale enabled evaluation of the model ability to quantitatively represent this slow process.
source: The possibility to experimentally modulate the ARTR persistence time scale further enabled us to evaluate the model ability to quantitatively represent this slow process.
evidence: This explains the value of the temperature manipulation.

claim: The ARTR is part of a widely distributed hindbrain network that controls the eye horizontal saccadic movements.
source: The ARTR is part of a widely distributed hindbrain network that controls the eye horizontal saccadic movements, and which includes several other neuronal populations whose activity is tuned to the eye velocity or position (Joshua and Lisberger, 2015; Wolf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader circuit context with citations.

claim: A possible extension of the model would consist in incorporating other nuclei to obtain a more complete representation of the oculomotor circuit.
source: A possible extension of the model would consist in incorporating these nuclei in order to obtain a more complete representation of the oculomotor circuit.
evidence: This is a prospective statement about future work.

claim: A similar data-driven approach could be implemented to capture the slow concerted dynamics that characterize numerous neural assemblies in the zebrafish brain.
